content.introduction: The Fed's next meeting is scheduled for June 16-17, 2026. The Federal Open Market Committee holds eight meetings annually to set monetary policy. The most recent meeting was on April 28-29, 2026.
body: ## ​The next scheduled FOMC (Federal Open Market Committee) meeting will be on April 28–29, 2026. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meets eight scheduled times a year to discuss and set monetary policy, and its decisions have a major impact on financial markets, mortgage rates, and economic growth. ## What is the FOMC? The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) is the branch of the Federal Reserve responsible for setting monetary policy for the US. ## What date is the next FOMC meeting? The Federal Reserve has scheduled its next FOMC meeting for April 28–29, 2026. At the end of each meeting, the FOMC announces its decisions on U.S. interest rates, followed by a press conference led by the Federal Reserve Chair. At its **March 18, 2026** meeting, the FOMC **kept the target range for the federal funds rate unchanged** **at 3.50% to 3.75%**. The Federal Open Market Committee is composed of twelve members, each with expertise in economics and monetary policy.

The [most recent meeting](https://www.forbes.com/sites/tylerroush/2026/04/29/fed-holds-interest-rates-steady-in-powells-last-meeting-with-most-dissenting-votes-since-1992/) was in April. Government policies and activities, such as tariffs and the war against Iran, have created uncertainty with implications like higher energy that would “push up overall inflation,” as Fed Chair Jerome Powell said in the press conference after the March 2026 FOMC meeting. Each of the FOMC’s 19 officials, seven more than the 12 FOMC voting members, submits their individual projections of gross domestic product (GDP) growth, the unemployment rate and inflation for the current year, as well as for the following two and then for the “longer run.” The inflation figures used are the Personal Consumption Expenditures produced by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, which is the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation. For each year, 2026 through 2028, and then the longer run, the dots show how the 19 Fed executives projected the midpoint of the federal funds rate range for each year.
